opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, especially now that I'm advising students myself.

I think the first thing is taste. It's hard to define, but it's the ability to tell which problems actually matter and which are just incremental or fashionable. In our field, especially in AI right now, there's a huge amount of noise. Thousands of papers come out every week. A good researcher has to look at all that and sense where the real bottleneck is, what's worth spending two or three years of your life on. Taste is partly intuition and partly accumulated experience. You build it by reading a lot, doing a lot of experiments, and failing a lot.

The second thing is something like courage, or independence. Once you have a judgment, you need to be willing to go against the consensus. A lot of the most important work, looking back, seemed unfashionable or even a bit stupid when people started on it. If you're always optimizing for what reviewers will like this cycle, you'll do fine, but you probably won't do something that changes how people think.

Third, and people underrate this, is being very hands-on. I still think a researcher has to really touch the data, run the code, look at the failure cases one by one. A lot of insight comes from those small, boring details that never make it into the paper. If you only stay at the level of ideas and slides, you lose contact with reality.

And then there's persistence and a kind of emotional stability. Research is mostly failure. Most of your ideas won't work. You need to be able to stay curious and keep going without getting crushed, but you also need to know when to let go of something. That balance is really hard.

Finally, I'd say communication and collaboration. Science today is rarely a solo thing. Being able to explain your ideas clearly, write well, and work with people who have different strengths is a big part of having impact.

If I had to pick just one, though, I'd say taste. Technical skill can be learned fairly quickly now, but knowing what question to ask is still the rarest thing.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should use their own judgment, be willing to go against consensus, and avoid choosing work just to satisfy reviewers or follow fashion.

r002.rationale: It defines research taste as distinguishing important problems from incremental or fashionable ones, and describes using that sense while evaluating the flood of research papers.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because I've watched students grow and partly because I keep asking it of myself.

I'd start with taste. It sounds vague, but I mean something concrete: the ability to look at a hundred possible problems and know which two or three are actually worth your time. Taste is knowing what matters before the field agrees it matters. When we were working on ConvNeXt, the question wasn't "can we beat a benchmark," it was "is the Transformer's advantage really about architecture, or is it about training recipes we've been quietly ignoring?" Picking that question was most of the work.

Second, I'd say the courage to be simple. Research culture rewards complexity because complexity looks like effort. But the results that last are almost always the ones where someone stripped something down and showed the core idea plainly. That's hard, because simplifying exposes you. If your simple thing fails, there's nowhere to hide.

Third is a kind of stubborn skepticism toward your own results. Most of the time, when an experiment looks too good, it is. A top researcher is the first person to try to break their own finding, not the last. The people I admire most treat their own conviction as a hypothesis.

Then there's execution, which people underrate. Having an idea is cheap. Being able to get a large-scale experiment running correctly, debug it when the loss curve does something strange at 3 a.m., and iterate fast enough to actually learn something before your intuition goes stale, that's a real skill, and it compounds.

And finally, honestly, communication. If you can't explain why something matters in a way that changes how other people think, the work only half exists. A lot of good ideas died because the author couldn't tell the story.

If I had to compress it: know what to work on, make it simple, doubt yourself productively, build fast, and explain well. Nobody has all five in equal measure. The good news is that most of them can be learned, and the one that seems most innate, taste, is really just the accumulated residue of having been wrong many times and paying attention.

r001.rationale: The response advocates choosing worthwhile problems before the field agrees, but does not clearly say a researcher should avoid choosing directions solely because others are interested in them.

r002.rationale: It discusses recognizing important problems, but does not connect that ability to reading research literature.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most important abilities is knowing how to ask a good question. There are many problems you can work on, and many ways to improve an existing method, but choosing a question that matters—and recognizing why it matters—is much harder.

Then you need the ability to turn that question into something concrete. Can you design an experiment that actually tests your idea? If the result is unexpected, can you figure out what it tells you, rather than just keep tuning until the number goes up? That requires technical depth, but also honesty about your own assumptions.

And I think you need both persistence and flexibility. Research involves spending a lot of time being wrong. You have to stay with a problem long enough to understand it, while remaining willing to abandon your favorite explanation. Having strong intuition is useful, but being able to revise that intuition is just as important.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should choose questions that matter, but does not say to avoid choosing directions solely because others are interested in them.

r002.rationale: The response discusses recognizing why a question matters, but does not mention reading research literature or distinguishing important findings from unimportant ones.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most important abilities is having good taste in research—being able to identify a problem that really matters. There are so many things you could work on, and being technically strong doesn’t automatically tell you which direction is worth pursuing.

Then you need the ability to turn that intuition into something concrete. Can you design a simple experiment that tests your idea? And when the result comes back, can you look at it honestly, especially if it contradicts what you hoped would happen?

I also think independence and openness have to go together. You need enough conviction to pursue an idea before everyone agrees with it, but you also need to listen and change your mind. That balance is difficult. Persistence matters, but you want to persist in understanding the problem, rather than just defending your original solution.

r001.rationale: The response says a researcher should identify problems that matter and pursue ideas before everyone agrees, but it does not say to avoid choosing directions solely because others are interested in them.

r002.rationale: The response discusses judging which research problems are worth pursuing, but does not connect that ability to reading research literature or distinguishing important from unimportant work there.
